newsitem.title: UK: Brown's big task--rate policy in boom/bust Britain.
newsitem.headline: Brown's big task--rate policy in boom/bust Britain.

text.p: Gordon Brown, Britain's finance minister in waiting, faces the daunting task of eradicating the boom-bust cycle that for Britain has produced one of the most volatile interest rate policies in the Group of Seven nations.
As Labour stormed to victory for the first time in 18 years, economists on Friday said Brown's biggest challenges was how to tame a robust economy without resorting to extremes.
Some said Brown will try to use a tighter tax policy to augment a few modest interest rate increases.

Others believe he could stamp his foot down with an early half-percentage point squeeze, pushing base rates up to 6.50 percent from their current six percent, and then follow up with more rate rises later in the year.

But the one common theme among analysts was that Brown would not do anything too radical -- he has spent a long time warming financial markets to the idea of his holding the reins and he will not want to do anything to stir up money dealers.

"There won't be any dramatic shift in policy, just an endorsement of the tough fiscal stance and a commitment to tackle inflation by raising interest rates," said Gerard Lyons, chief economist, DKB International.

In the past decade, British interest rates have swung from 15 percent to less than six percent. Meanwhile the economy has gone fron a runaway boom in the late 1980s to the worst recession since the 1930s depression. That recession, which ended in 1992, has left deep scars on Britain's industrial landscape and its people.

Now, the economy is expanding at a rate of three percent per year and economists are predicting growth rising towards four percent. That compared with average trend growth in the economy during the past four decades of 2.25 to 2.50 percent.

The Bank of England, which must take orders from the government on monetary policy, has been calling for a monetary tightening for months as evidence of inflationary pressures and strong consumer-led growth have been building.

But there are wide divisions over how much tightening is needed. As Britain's devastated manufacturing sector has been finding its feet in the past few years, thanks partly to improving exports, industrialists have argued against harsh measures which could set the nation's producers back again.
Instead, many want Brown to use fiscal policy, coupled with the dampening effect of a strong pound, to rein in the economy.
"The real issue for rates is going to be how much, and how fiscal policy is going to tighten," said Sean Shepley, economist at Credit Suisse First Boston.
"The market has priced in a series of tightenings over the next 12 months and if they do tighten fiscal policy, there is probably too much tightening (on rates) priced in," he said.

As of Thursday, British interest rate futures, short sterling contracts, pointed to base lending rates of seven percent by the end of 1997. In this year alone, market expectations of where end-1997 rates would be have strayed from 6-3/4 percent to 7-1/2 percent.

As results were streaming in, Brown said he would move swiftly on his first budget. "I have said the budget will be within two months," he said, adding the party would not renege on its pledge not to raise the main rates of British income tax, rates which the Conservatives had steadily cut since 1979.

British data have been showing strong, consumer-led growth for months and with money supply expansion in double digits and wage increases rising, many economists said an interest rate rise is needed quickly to stem inflationary pressures.

Economists are also fretting over the potential fallout from more than 20 billion pounds ($32.5 billion) of free shares which are being given to consumers as a number of British home loan institutions convert into banks.
For these reasons and more, economists say Brown should listen to Bank of England governor Eddie George when he asks for pre-emptive moves on interest rates.
"Politically it makes sense for the new Chancellor to take the Bank of England's advice on interest rates," said Sean Shepley, economist at Credit Suisse First Boston.
"We know that Eddie George has been pushing for a quarter point hike now for about six months."
Brown early on Friday also reaffirmed his commitment to the government's 2.5 percent inflation target. British core inflation is currently just over that, at 2.7 percent.
Some argue the Brown should give the economy a double-whammy of fiscal and monetary tightening.

"They'll need to show some kind of policy credibility very quickly in terms of a hike in the base rate and ideally a tight budget as well," said Jeremy Hawkins, senior economic advisor at Bank of America in London.
